editorNote: Extra Edition: the graphical desktop has become a shipping IBM PC product, even as rival window systems line up for 1984.
morningLine: Visi On reaches the IBM PC, Nintendo sends Donkey Kong Jr. to arithmetic class, and the home-computer price war begins to cool.

lead.headline: The Window Wars Reach the IBM PC
lead.dek: Visi On ships a commercial graphical desktop while Microsoft and Quarterdeck ready cheaper rivals.
body: VisiCorp has put a windowed, mouse-driven working environment onto the IBM Personal Computer, turning a laboratory-style graphical interface into a commercial product. Visi On joins word processing, spreadsheet and graphing programs behind one visual system, giving business users a consistent way to move among tasks.

The elegance comes with demanding requirements. Applications must be written especially for Visi On, and the development system requires a costly minicomputer toolchain. Serious windowing also calls for roughly half a megabyte of memory and a hard disk, pushing a complete installation toward the expensive end of the PC market.

Microsoft is promising a different bargain for mid-1984. Its proposed Windows extension, projected at $100 to $250, uses tiled rather than overlapping windows and aims to standardize how programs address displays across machines. Microsoft president William Gates describes a neat-desk metaphor, a deliberate contrast with overlapping papers.

Quarterdeck’s DESQ, due in January, offers a third route: windows around most existing text-mode DOS applications without rewriting them. Graphics programs would still take over the full screen, but compatibility could matter more than visual polish to owners with established software libraries.

The contest is bigger than window decoration. Each company is bidding to control the common language between users, applications and displays. As analyst Egil Juliussen puts it, 1984 may determine who becomes the “window master of the world.”

stories.headline: Home-Computer Price War Finally Cools
body: After a year of punishing markdowns, manufacturers at COMDEX expect the steep slide in computer prices to moderate. Machines had been falling 20 to 25 percent annually, with even sharper cuts below $1,000; Texas Instruments has now quit the home-computer field and Atari has accumulated heavy losses.

IBM’s $700-to-$1,300 PCjr gives rivals room to retreat from the bottom. Atari and Coleco raised prices after its unveiling, while shortages of common PC components leave clone makers with little reason to discount. Kaypro president David Kay dissents, arguing that Japanese vendors may still move into the gap beneath PCjr.

stories.headline: Donkey Kong Jr. Clambers Into Arithmetic
body: Nintendo released Donkey Kong Jr. Math for the Family Computer in Japan on December 12. The ¥4,500 cartridge turns the familiar vine-climbing action into addition, subtraction, multiplication and division exercises, asking players to collect numbers and symbols.
Developed by Nintendo R&D1, it follows November’s Popeye English-learning title and shows how console makers hope recognizable arcade characters can broaden the family market beyond action games.

stories.headline: A Christmas Bounce for Atari Amid the Crash
body: Electronic Games Hotline led its December 18 number with an upbeat report that Atari hardware and software sales were booming for Christmas. The headline offers a rare bright patch in a year defined by excess cartridges, retailer caution and company losses.

The holiday lift does not erase the industry’s damage: Mattel has just reported a large quarterly loss and Atari’s computer division remains under pressure. But it suggests strong brands and attractive seasonal pricing can still move machines and games even in a contracting market.

stories.headline: Software Moves from Boxes to Parcels
body: Publishers are experimenting with splitting programs into modules and bundling related applications as software grows more costly to develop. Peachtree and Information Unlimited Software offer packages at roughly half the total price of their separate components.

Price itself has become a marketing signal. Business Systems raised an Apple II integrated package from $79 to $179 after deciding buyers equated cheap software with weak software, while Lotus 1-2-3 holds at $495 and VisiCalc has fallen to $250.
